module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Mathoverflow 21003

Is there any polynomial $f(x, y) \in \mathbb{Q}[x, y]$ such that
$f : \mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}$ is a bijection?

*Reference:* [mathoverflow/21003](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/21003)
asked by user [*Z.H.*](https://mathoverflow.net/users/5098/z-h)
-/

@[expose] public section

open scoped Polynomial


namespace Mathoverflow21003

/--
Is there any polynomial $f(x, y) \in \mathbb{Q}[x, y]$ such that
$f : \mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}$ is a bijection?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 12]
theorem mathoverflow_21003 :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ f : MvPolynomial (Fin 2) ℚ, Function.Bijective fun x ↦ f.eval x := by
  sorry

end Mathoverflow21003

reformulations.difference: The source's map is f : ℚ × ℚ → ℚ. The Lean statement uses the domain `Fin 2 → ℚ` and writes the map as `fun x ↦ f.eval x`. Lean elaborates this to `(MvPolynomial.eval x) f`: dot notation passes the polynomial to the coerced ring hom, and the point comes first.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: `finTwoArrowEquiv ℚ : (Fin 2 → ℚ) ≃ ℚ × ℚ` sends x to (x 0, x 1). Under this equivalence, `fun x ↦ MvPolynomial.eval x f` corresponds to `fun p ↦ MvPolynomial.eval ![p.1, p.2] f`, i.e. (a, b) ↦ f(a, b) with X 0 ↦ a and X 1 ↦ b. Composing with an equivalence preserves bijectivity in both directions. So `∃ f, Bijective (fun x ↦ f.eval x)` holds exactly when `∃ f, Bijective (fun p : ℚ × ℚ ↦ eval ![p.1, p.2] f)` does. I proved this `↔` in Lean.

review.notes: The single declaration faithfully states MathOverflow 21003. The `answer(sorry)` slot has type Prop, sits before all quantifiers, and the right-hand side poses the existence question the same way round as the source (not a negated conjecture). I checked in Lean how `f.eval x` elaborates (`(MvPolynomial.eval x) f`, x : Fin 2 → ℚ). I proved the equivalence with the literal ℚ × ℚ formulation. I ran sanity checks: an evaluation computes as expected, and X0 + X1 is shown not bijective. The status `research open` is correct. Only conditional results exist: Poonen 2010 gives an injective polynomial assuming Bombieri–Lang, a different question. Bresciani (Amer. J. Math. 2025), implementing Tao's 2019 polymath strategy, rules out polynomial bijections assuming weak Bombieri–Lang. No unconditional resolution found. If the problem is settled unconditionally, the expected answer is answer(False). Optional metadata remark, not a defect: the question is filed under number theory on MO, so AMS 11 (or 14) could be added alongside AMS 12.
